title: A Giant Computer Simulation Lights Up the Universe's Dark Age
summary:
Imagine the universe as a dark room with no lights switched on. That is how the early cosmos looked during a stretch scientists call the cosmic dark age — and a powerful new computer simulation called Lumina is helping researchers explore it.

Developed by scientists at MIT, Harvard University, and other institutions, Lumina recreates about 2 billion years of cosmic history across a region roughly 1.6 billion light-years wide. It tracks dark matter, gas, stars, and light, showing how the first galaxies formed and how radiation spread through space.

The story begins with the Big Bang, when the universe was hot and dense, packed with electrons and other particles. As it expanded and cooled, electrons joined atomic nuclei to form neutral hydrogen. About 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the universe entered its dark age: there were no stars yet to light it, and the hydrogen filling space could soak up ultraviolet light.

Then the first stars and galaxies appeared, and everything changed. Their ultraviolet light knocked electrons off hydrogen atoms, a process called re-ionization. As more hydrogen was re-ionized, the universe grew clearer, letting light travel much farther.

Lumina also follows a second, tougher change: helium re-ionization. Stripping electrons from helium takes far more energetic radiation, and the results suggest that actively feeding supermassive black holes supplied it, while stars and galaxies handled the hydrogen.

MIT physics professor Mark Vogelsberger says Lumina covers star and galaxy formation as well as the re-ionization of hydrogen and helium, in a volume 100 times larger than previous best simulations.

Lumina builds on an earlier simulation called IllustrisTNG and adds a model of how light travels through space. The team is sharing it with other scientists, so its predictions can be checked against observations from telescopes now and in the future.
why_it_matters: Lumina lets scientists test how the first galaxies lit up the universe and cleared its darkness, and its predictions can now be checked against telescope observations, deepening our understanding of how the cosmos we live in came to be.

The process in which light knocked electrons off atoms, making space clearer for light to travel.
Hydrogen gas whose atoms still hold their electrons, so it can soak up some kinds of light.
Extremely massive black holes at the centers of galaxies that can give off very energetic radiation while feeding.

background_read: The cosmic dark age was the long stretch after the early universe cooled enough for electrons to join atomic nuclei and form neutral hydrogen, leaving no stars to shine light through space. Hydrogen gas filled the universe and could soak up ultraviolet light, so the cosmos stayed dark until the first stars and galaxies formed. When those first stars and galaxies appeared, their ultraviolet light knocked electrons off hydrogen atoms in a process called re-ionization, gradually making the universe clearer so light could travel farther. Helium needed far more energetic radiation to lose its electrons, and scientists think actively feeding supermassive black holes supplied that energy while stars and galaxies handled the hydrogen.
